### MEDIUM: Docs now say missing risk\-receipt evidence does not block a basic serving grant, contradicting the threat model
[docs/architecture/security/attestation\.md:106](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/d-inference/blob/25e7a78890b35e7d9f3972ba4668c412d8503239/docs/architecture/security/attestation.md#L106) · A-016, T-053, T-057, TB-011

The replaced paragraph defers to an external darkbloom\-platform contract\. It says missing receipt or risk evidence "alone does not clear an accepted, otherwise valid basic grant" and that only reward and MDM\-removal readiness are withheld\. The canonical model \(TB\-011, T\-053, T\-057\) and the removed base text require a fresh verified risk receipt with a complete metric for every serving grant\. If the coordinator follows the new text, a credential with unverified or absent receipt evidence stays routable, and receipt monitoring stops being a serving gate\. A provider could then withhold or fail receipt renewal and keep serving\. The threat model has no entry for "basic grant" versus "reward\-ready" authorization\. Its mitigations for A\-016, T\-053 and T\-057 should be updated or the docs corrected\. The in\-repo link to provider\-authorization\.md was also replaced by a pinned external\-repo URL that this PR cannot verify\. Fix: reconcile the threat model and its source\-of\-truth reference, and state which policy this repo's coordinator enforces\.

findings.detail: The PR rewrites the attestation Context paragraph to follow a platform contract. Under it, missing recurring receipt/risk evidence "neither blocks otherwise qualified basic serving nor adds assertions". It also lets an established exact identity "retain last-known policy" when administrative reads fail, up to the proof and administrative ceilings. The canonical threat model (TB-011, T-053/T-055/T-057, header notes) still says every serving grant needs a fresh verified risk receipt, and treats receipts as part of the sybil/continuity defense. The PR does not touch threat-model.yaml, although a changelog line claims the retained threat model stays aligned. The assumptions are now inconsistent. Basic serving can proceed without receipt evidence, which weakens the throttle on credential rotation and fake-machine inflation (T-055). Revocation or denial can lag by the retained-policy window when reads fail (T-053). Fix: update TB-011 and T-053/T-055/T-057, plus A-016, to the receipt-optional basic grant. State the maximum retained-policy and revocation lag, and keep reward and MDM-removal readiness explicitly receipt-gated. Alternatively, mark the doc text as a platform-repo contract that is not yet adopted here.
findings.title: Docs adopt receipt-optional basic serving, but the threat model still requires a verified risk receipt

findings.detail: The head text (lines 10-14, 112) says the external darkbloom-platform contract supersedes the retained coordinator snapshot. Basic serving is no longer blocked by missing recurring receipt/risk evidence. An established exact identity may retain last-known policy within the original ceilings, and receipt monitoring is split from `EvaluateAuthorization`. The canonical threat model still states that every serving grant needs a fresh verified risk receipt. It also relies on failed reads never extending authorization (T-053, T-057, TB-011, A-016). A provider with a revoked or risky credential, or one whose receipt/risk evidence is withheld or failing, could keep serving under last-known policy during admin-read or receipt outages until the ceilings expire. This is documented as the linked platform revision's behavior and not as deployed, so adoption is uncertain. The threat model needs updating to state the new freshness and ceiling assumptions and how revocation fences interact with retained policy. The docs should also say which repository enforces them, since the in-repo coordinator snapshot is now explicitly non-authoritative.
findings.title: Docs adopt platform semantics that drop the per-grant fresh risk receipt and allow last-known-policy retention; threat model still asserts the stricter rule

findings.detail: Head lines 69-76 describe an `app_attest_endpoint_resumption` candidate. `CoordinatorClient` answers it directly with the fixed process key and a socket nonce, without Apple work. A matching platform could then use that response together with retained evidence to resume or bind authorization to a new endpoint or connection. This differs from the previously documented requirement for a fresh current-endpoint assertion on every connection and endpoint binding. The threat model does not cover the new surface: a replayed or misbound custody response, a proof signed by the process key alone with no hardware-bound Apple freshness, a provider-side oracle that signs coordinator-supplied nonces, and deadline preservation. The threat model should add this path to TB-011, T-053 and T-054 and fix the required properties. The nonce must be single-use and bound to the connection and endpoint, original proof deadlines must not be extended, and revocation and qualification checks must be re-run at resume.
findings.title: New endpoint-resumption custody response is attack surface not covered by the threat model

findings.detail: The new identity-binding.md section documents a provider-side responder that answers a coordinator 'resume' challenge with the in-memory X25519 key. It also references backend 'retained-proof' checks that are 'platform-owned' and may not be deployed. This is a new way to re-establish a serving binding without a fresh Apple assertion. TB-011, T-053 (replayed proof or stale authorization after a connection change) and T-057 do not describe it. Nothing in the model covers the nonce and socket binding, single use, the retained-proof lifetime limit, the revocation fence, or the case where a provider ships the responder before the coordinator counterpart exists. A stale or replayed resume challenge on a replacement socket, or a retained proof outliving revocation, would extend serving authorization. Fix: add the resume path to TB-011 and T-053 with explicit invariants (fresh per-socket nonce, one answer, proof age cap, revocation and qualification-generation recheck at final handoff, no lease extension).
findings.title: App Attest same-process endpoint resumption is a new authorization-adjacent path outside the threat model

findings.detail: Provider logout now sends the raw bearer token to POST /v1/device/revoke. The docs say backend revocation policy and persistence are 'platform-owned' and that local deletion cannot invalidate a copy held elsewhere, with an offline warning. This adds an unauthenticated-by-session bearer-in-request control-plane endpoint and a state where a deleted token stays valid on the coordinator. A thief holding a copied provider token (A-008) can keep registering as that account's provider, and the endpoint itself could be abused to revoke tokens if the token is leaked. The model has no threat for provider-token lifecycle: revoke endpoint rate-limiting, token-in-body or header logging, revocation idempotency, immediate effect on live connections bound by B6, and what happens when offline logout leaves the token active. Fix: add a threat and mitigations for A-008 token revocation, including terminating or rebinding existing sessions on revocation.
findings.title: New provider-token revocation endpoint and logout flow are not covered by the threat model

findings.detail: The new test.md sections describe 'Stage C' resumption: a provider reconnects after a 125-second transport break with an unchanged process, endpoint and engine, and with 'unchanged load and Apple assertion counters'. The canonical TB-011, T-053 and A-016 say serving authorization is bound to one current connection and endpoint. They also say each serving grant needs a fresh assertion and a new verified receipt, and that stale authorization must not survive a connection change. A resume path that skips a new Apple assertion and re-binds an old grant to a new socket (only a 'fresh socket nonce') is a different trust transition. A malicious provider (ADV-001), or anyone holding a captured resume token or proof, could exploit it if the binding, expiry, reflection protection or revocation-fencing rules are weak. The PR changes only docs, so I cannot confirm the code. TB-011, T-053 and the logout and credential-revocation behaviour need explicit entries for resumption: what is authenticated, the maximum window, and how revocation or a policy-generation change invalidates a resumable grant. Suggested fix: update the threat model with these properties, or confirm in the docs that resumption never extends the grant lease and never survives revocation or a generation change.
findings.title: Docs describe provider endpoint resumption across reconnect, but the App Attest threat model is not updated

findings.detail: The head text says a missing or unverified recurring risk receipt, or a missing risk metric, 'does not clear an accepted, otherwise valid basic serving grant'. It also says no extra assertions are required. It defers to a pinned external platform doc and adds that not every deployment uses the policy. The canonical TB-011 and the base docs require a verified fresh risk receipt for every serving grant, and receipt expiry and renewal deadlines shorten the grant. If the platform coordinator follows the new text, grants could outlive receipt verification. That weakens the credential-continuity and revocation signal (T-053, T-055). Operators and reviewers also cannot tell which policy is live. Fix: update TB-011, A-016 and T-053/T-055 to define the basic-serving versus rewards/MDM-removal receipt split and its bounds. Alternatively, keep the docs aligned with the current requirement until that policy ships.
findings.title: Docs describe a recurring risk-receipt policy that conflicts with the canonical serving requirement

findings.detail: The added text describes a same-process reconnect in which the provider answers an encrypted endpoint-resumption challenge without another Apple call. The platform then rechecks retained evidence and policy. This creates a serving-authorization path that skips fresh assertion verification, which TB-011 treats as required (assertion, nonce and counter, current endpoint and connection binding). The docs themselves note the path is not enabled in production and rely on a report whose content was not supplied. Risks include replaying or rebinding an old grant to a new connection, and extending a grant past the 15-minute freshness window, past receipt expiry, or past revocation after a credential or build change (T-053, T-054). Fix: add the resumption protocol to TB-011/T-053, with explicit bounds on the maximum total lifetime without Apple proof, fencing by revocation and policy generation, endpoint-key binding, and the final-handoff check. Keep it disabled until then.
findings.title: New endpoint-resumption path serves without a fresh Apple call; not covered by the threat model

findings.detail: The new logout flow (documented only; the Swift code was not provided) captures the coordinator from the running provider's state, including a `start --coordinator` override. If there is no live snapshot, it falls back to the config file. After shutdown it sends the raw saved provider token as `Authorization: Bearer` to `POST /v1/device/revoke` at that coordinator. The docs say it uses a 10s timeout and follows no redirects. They do not say it requires `https`, or that it derives the HTTP origin from the `wss://` URL in the same way as the provider connection. A plaintext or attacker-chosen coordinator value in the override, state file or config would leak the long-lived provider token (A-008) during a routine logout. Because logout is meant to invalidate the credential, a leak at that point is especially unwelcome. The threat model has no entry for this new token-transmission path. Fix: enforce TLS and the same coordinator origin and allow-list as the provider WebSocket, refuse non-https URLs, and add this path to the TB-002/A-008 analysis.
findings.title: Logout sends the raw provider bearer token to a coordinator URL taken from local state, with no stated scheme or host check
